name: Application subclass
syntax: public class App extends Application { @Override public void start(Stage stage) { ... } }
desc: Every JavaFX program starts with a class that extends Application and overrides start. The toolkit creates one instance with the no-argument constructor and calls start on the FX thread.
body:
`start` receives a stage that is already created but empty and invisible. Build the root node, wrap it in a `Scene`, attach the scene, then call `show()`.

Put file reading in `init()` or in a plain helper class. Keeping the GUI class thin means the data code can run without a display.

name: launch()
desc: Boots the JavaFX toolkit, constructs the application instance, and runs the lifecycle. Call it once from main; a second call throws IllegalStateException.

name: init()
desc: Runs once before start on the launcher thread. Use it for slow or risky work such as reading a file, and never create controls here.
body:
An exception thrown in `init` prevents the window from appearing, and the stack trace shows up as an application startup failure. Wrap file access in `try` and store the error message for an `Alert` in `start`.

For exam tasks the method is optional. It becomes useful when the file is large and the window should appear only after the data is ready.

name: stop()
desc: Runs after the last window closes or after Platform.exit(). Use it to flush data or stop threads, never to ask the user a question.
body:
For a save prompt use `stage.setOnCloseRequest` and call `event.consume()` when the user cancels. `stop` is for cleanup only.

If `Platform.setImplicitExit(false)` was called, `stop` runs only when `Platform.exit()` is called explicitly.

name: Stage.setScene() and show()
desc: Attaches the scene to the window and makes the window visible. Nothing is drawn before show() runs.
body:
Order matters for sizing. Setting the scene first lets the stage compute its size from the scene; changing the root afterwards needs `stage.sizeToScene()` if the window should follow.

A stage without a scene throws no error on `show()` in older versions but shows an empty window. Always attach the scene.

name: Stage window settings
desc: Sets the title bar text, the smallest size the user may drag to, and whether the window can be resized. The minimum size protects a fixed layout from clipping.
body:
A window cannot be made smaller than the sum of the minimum sizes of its content plus padding and spacing. If the stage refuses to shrink even though `setMinWidth` is small, look at the children's `minWidth` values.

Icons are set with `stage.getIcons().add(new Image(...))`. The exam rarely asks for one; a missing image path throws at startup, so skip it unless required.

name: Second window
desc: Creates another window with its own scene. The owner keeps it above the main window, and the modality decides which windows are blocked while it is open.
body:
`WINDOW_MODAL` blocks the owner only. `APPLICATION_MODAL` blocks every window of the application. `Modality.NONE` is the default and behaves like an independent window.

For a message or a single question, use `Alert` instead. A hand-built dialog needs its own buttons and its own close handling, which is three times the code for the same result.

name: new Scene()
desc: Wraps the root node into a scene with an initial content size. The scene holds the root, the size, the fill colour and the stylesheets.
body:
The constructor without a width and height uses the preferred size of the root, which is often too small or too large by accident. Pass both numbers when the task names a size.

A node already attached to another scene must be removed from its parent first, because one node has one parent.

name: Scene switching
desc: Replaces the content of the current window without creating a new one. Build both scenes once and reuse them.
body:
Swapping scenes loses nothing that is stored outside the scene, so keep shared state in fields or in a small model class. Rebuilding a scene on every switch resets its controls.

When only part of the screen changes, replace the centre of a `BorderPane` instead. The menu bar and the status line then stay attached and keep their handlers.

name: Add a stylesheet
desc: Loads a CSS file for one scene. The URL must point at the file on the classpath and must not be null.
body:
`getClass().getResource("app.css")` looks in the package of the class. The leading slash means the classpath root, which is where Maven puts `src/main/resources`.

A wrong path returns `null` and `toExternalForm()` throws `NullPointerException` before the window opens. Guard it while developing, and keep the guard in exam code so a missing file costs styling time only.

name: Button action
desc: Runs the handler when the button is clicked or when it is the default button and Enter is pressed. Reading control values inside the lambda is what makes the form work.
body:
`setOnAction` replaces the previous handler. If a button and a menu item must run different code, give them separate lambdas that call one shared method.

When two handlers must both run, use `addEventHandler(ActionEvent.ACTION, ...)` instead of calling `setOnAction` twice.

name: TextField value
desc: Reads the typed text as a String. The prompt is grey hint text and is never returned by getText, so an empty field reads as an empty string, not null.

name: Wrapping label
desc: Makes long label text wrap instead of clipping. Wrapping needs a width limit, otherwise the label grows as wide as its text.
body:
Inside an `HBox` the label also needs `HBox.setHgrow` or a fixed width, because the row does not shrink a child below its preferred width on its own.

For a whole block of text with several paragraphs, use a `TextArea` with `setEditable(false)` and `setWrapText(true)`.

name: CheckBox
desc: Returns the current state of the box. Check boxes are independent; a group of them needs no ToggleGroup.
body:
`selectedProperty()` is observable when a label or another control must react immediately:

```java
summary.textProperty().bind(
    Bindings.when(extraBed.selectedProperty())
            .then("Extra bed requested")
            .otherwise("No extra bed"));
```

name: RadioButton with ToggleGroup
desc: Radio buttons in one ToggleGroup allow exactly one selection. Attach every button and select one before the window is shown.
body:
The `null` guard matters. Clicking the selected radio button can clear the group, and then `byYear.isSelected()` and `byHotel.isSelected()` are both false.

Reading the selection inside the handler with `if (byYear.isSelected())` is clearer than comparing toggle objects, and it survives a later redesign that adds a third mode.

name: ComboBox
desc: A drop-down list with one selected value. The value is null until the user or the code sets one.
body:
`setValue` selects an item and also accepts values that are not in the list, which is useful for a free-text combo after `setEditable(true)`.

For a long list, `setVisibleRowCount(8)` keeps the popup short. For typed filtering, make it editable and read `getEditor().getText()`.

name: DatePicker
desc: Returns the chosen date as a LocalDate, or null when the field is empty. It does not validate ranges for you.
body:
The text shown in the editor follows the locale, while `getValue()` is locale independent. Parse data files with `LocalDate.parse` and let the picker handle display.

`setEditable(false)` stops the user from typing a date in a format the parser does not expect.

name: Spinner with an integer range
desc: A numeric field with arrows and a bounded range. getValue returns an Integer, so no parsing is needed.
body:
A bare `new Spinner<>(1, 10, 2)` also compiles in recent JavaFX versions, but the value factory form shows the intended range and works on every supported version.

With `setEditable(true)`, text that is outside the range is rejected and the previous value returns. If the user typed a value and clicked Save directly, the focus loss commits it before the handler runs.

name: ListView items
desc: Replaces the whole content of the list. Use clear() plus addAll() when appending, and setAll() when the old rows must disappear.
body:
Backing the list with an `ObservableList` keeps it in sync with the data:

```java
ObservableList<Booking> bookings = FXCollections.observableArrayList();
bookings.addAll(loadBookings(file));   // the list redraws itself
```

`setItems` swaps the backing list. Calling it twice is fine, but a listener attached to the old list stops seeing changes.

name: ListView selection listener
desc: Fires when the selected row changes, including when the list is cleared and the value becomes null. This is the correct hook for showing details.
body:
Do not wire row clicks through a cell factory for selection. Cells are recycled while scrolling, and a cell that shows row 40 may later show row 3.

To preselect a row, call `getSelectionModel().select(index)` after the items are set. `selectFirst()` is a shortcut for the first row.

name: TableView column
desc: Binds a column to one field of the row object. The factory is called for every visible cell, so it must stay cheap.
body:
`PropertyValueFactory("city")` needs a `getCity()` method. Java records have `city()`, so the explicit wrapper is the reliable option for records. `asObject()` is required on `ReadOnlyIntegerWrapper` when the column type is `Integer`.

Column widths: `setPrefWidth(180)` per column, and `table.setColumnResizePolicy(TableView.CONSTRAINED_RESIZE_POLICY_FLEX_LAST_COLUMN)` to fill the table width. The older `CONSTRAINED_RESIZE_POLICY` constant is deprecated in JavaFX 20 and later.

name: Alert
desc: Shows a standard dialog with one OK button. showAndWait blocks until it is closed, which is what a message or an error needs.

name: FileChooser open dialog
desc: Opens the native file dialog and returns the chosen File, or null when the user cancels. The null check is part of the pattern, not an optional extra.
body:
`showSaveDialog` returns a target file that may not exist yet, so write to `file.toPath()` rather than reading it.

Reading goes through `Files.readAllLines(file.toPath(), StandardCharsets.UTF_8)` or `Files.newBufferedReader`. Keep the parsing in a method that accepts a `File` or `Path`, so it can be tested from `main` without opening a window.

Wrap the read in `try` and show the message in an `Alert` with `AlertType.ERROR`. A raw stack trace in the console is not a user-facing error path.

name: MenuItem and accelerator
desc: Adds a clickable command to a menu with an optional keyboard shortcut. Shortcut maps to Ctrl on Windows and Linux and Command on macOS.
body:
Use `Ctrl+O` only when the task explicitly says Ctrl, because that breaks the shortcut on macOS.

A menu item is not a node, so it cannot be added to a layout. It lives in a `Menu`, and the `Menu` lives in a `MenuBar` that is placed in the layout like any other control.

name: Platform.exit()
desc: Closes the toolkit and ends the application, running stop() on the way out. Use it for an Exit menu item and for cancelling a close request after a prompt.
body:
`System.exit(0)` also kills the process, but it skips `stop()` and can leave threads running. `Platform.exit()` is the supported path.

With `Platform.setImplicitExit(false)` the application keeps running after the last window closes, and then `Platform.exit()` is the only clean way to end it.

name: Platform.runLater()
desc: Queues a task on the FX thread. Any UI change from a background thread must go through it, otherwise JavaFX throws IllegalStateException.
body:
The exception text is `Not on FX application thread; currentThread = ...`. It appears the moment a control is touched, which is why the failing line is usually a setter, not the thread creation.

`Task` and `Service` wrap the same pattern with `setOnSucceeded` and progress properties. For one file load, the plain thread plus `Platform.runLater` is shorter and easier to defend in an exam.

name: Window close request
desc: Runs when the user tries to close the window, before it hides. Calling event.consume() cancels the close.
body:
This is the last moment where a question can be asked, because the window is still open. `stop()` runs too late for a dialog.

A confirmation with `Alert` returns an `Optional<ButtonType>`. Compare it to `ButtonType.OK` and consume the close event when the answer is no.

name: Style class
desc: Adds a CSS class to a node so a stylesheet can target it. One node can carry several classes, and every control already has its type class.

name: Inline style
desc: Applies CSS directly to one node. It beats the stylesheet, which makes it useful for a computed colour and dangerous for layout rules.
body:
Inline style has the highest priority short of a stylesheet `!important`. A value set here will not be overridden by a later theme change, so keep it for colours and weights that depend on data.

Only `-fx-` properties exist. `color`, `background`, `margin` and `padding` are silently ignored, which looks like the style did nothing.
